newsitem.title: UK: AGF could afford GAN without extra funds - Salomon.
newsitem.headline: AGF could afford GAN without extra funds - Salomon.

text.p: French insurer AGF could buy the soon-to-be-privatised GAN group without needing extra capital and without upsetting its own recovery, insurance analysts at Salomon Brothers said on Friday.
AGF's share price has languished over concerns about talk from chairman Antoine Jeancourt-Galignani of future acquisitions, with particular emphasis on GAN.
"While we acknowledge several legitimate investor concerns, we believe this event risk is now over discounted," analyst Brian Shea said.

"We do not believe AGF would need to raise fresh equity to buy GAN, and only modest cost savings are required for the deal to meet acceptable return on equity criteria and be strongly accretive to earnings," he said.

The French government recently confirmed plans to sell its 76 per cent stake in the troubled GAN group which lost 5.7 million francs last year because of bad real estate investments. A 20 billion franc rescue and sell-off plan announced by the previous government in February has sparked interest from several European insurers, including AGF.

Shea estimated that GAN was worth 8.5 billion francs. He calculated that AGF had a current war chest of about 5 billion francs, to which could be added 4.4 billion in convertible bond proceeds. Shea said AGF could also expand its debt level, currently standing at 44 per cent.
"Putting all this together we estimate that the company could afford an acquisition of up to 10 to 12 billion francs." Shea said.
Some market observers have criticised AGF for talking of acquisition when it is still in the midst of a recovery plan of its own.
"We are sympathetic with that view, but market forces and opportunism may not allow AGF that luxury, " said Shea.
"If AGF is right in thinking that AXA-UAP presents a formidable threat, it is best to address that without delay," he said.
The analyst added that AGF's earnings recovery was on track, and predicted a 17 percent increase in profits in 1997, a 30 percent increase in 1998, and a 10 percent increase in 1999.
